abstract:
Inflammation of the olfactory mucosa, rather than airflow obstruction, is a major barrier to olfactory recovery in chronic rhinosinusitis with olfactory dysfunction (CRSwOD). Macrophages, a predominant immune cell population in the olfactory mucosa, play a key role in regulating local inflammation and olfactory neuroregeneration.
This study aimed to investigate the role of Sirtuin 3 (SIRT3) in modulating macrophage function and its impact on olfactory recovery in CRSwOD.
Single-cell RNA sequencing, bulk RNA sequencing, and untargeted metabolomics data were analyzed to characterize immune and neuronal alterations in CRSwOD, with a focus on macrophage activation states. In vivo experiments using SIRT3-deficient mice were performed to evaluate olfactory sensory neuron (OSN) integrity, while in vitro assays examined the metabolic and inflammatory profiles of SIRT3-deficient macrophages under inflammatory conditions.
Transcriptomic analysis revealed that olfactory dysfunction was closely associated with the altered functional status of mucosal macrophages. During the progression of chronic rhinosinusitis in mice, loss of SIRT3 exacerbated OSN loss and impaired the protective role of macrophages in maintaining neuronal homeostasis. Mechanistically, SIRT3 deficiency enhanced macrophage proinflammatory activity, increased hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF-1α) expression, promoted glycolysis, and reduced mitochondrial membrane potential.
In a mouse model of chronic rhinosinusitis, SIRT3 modulates macrophage-mediated inflammatory metabolism within the olfactory mucosa, thereby protecting against inflammation-induced olfactory damage. These findings provide mechanistic insight into inflammation-driven olfactory dysfunction and identify SIRT3 as a potential therapeutic target for CRSwOD.
